overview.title: Parsing COCO annotations and normalizing boxes
overview.section: 12.2 Training a YOLO model from scratch
overview.main_topic: Downloading the COCO annotations JSON, joining boxes to images by image ID, and rescaling pixel boxes to a unit square
overview.central_idea: COCO stores images and box annotations separately, linked by image IDs. Listing 12.2 builds one record per image containing its file path, its list of boxes and its list of labels, converting each `x, y, width, height` pixel box into coordinates on a [0, 1] square so later code can ignore image sizes.

summary:
The page opens with the end of **listing 12.1**: after closing the image download, a second `keras.utils.get_file` call fetches `annotations_trainval2017.zip` (with `extract=True`) into `annotations_path`.

The authors then explain the "input massaging" needed. The first download is just an **unlabeled directory of images**; the second contains **all image metadata as a JSON file**. COCO assigns each image an ID and pairs each bounding box with one of these IDs, so the boxes must be **collated** with their images.

Each COCO box is given as **`x, y, width, height` in pixels, measured from the top-left corner**. While loading, the authors rescale boxes to points in a **`[0, 1]` unit square**, so later code can manipulate boxes without checking each image's size.

**Listing 12.2** does this:

1. Loads `instances_train2017.json`.
2. Builds `images`, a dict from image ID to image record (the callout says "Sorts image metadata by ID"; it is really an ID-indexed lookup table).
3. Defines `scale_box(box, width, height)`: multiplies all four values by `1 / max(width, height)` and shifts `x` (for portrait images) or `y` (for landscape images) by half of the size difference — exactly the coordinates the box would have if the image were **centred inside a square** of side max(width, height), then scaled to [0, 1].
4. Loops over every annotation, creating `{"boxes": [], "labels": []}` for a new `image_id`, appending the scaled box and the `category_id` label, and storing the image's file path under `images_path + "/train2017/"`.
5. Converts the dict to a list, `metadata`, one entry per image that has annotations.

The page ends with "Let's take a look at the data we just loaded", leading to listing 12.3 on p.358.

concepts.name: Bounding box (COCO xywh format)
concepts.definition: A rectangle given by its top-left corner (x, y) and its width and height, in pixels in raw COCO.
concepts.intuition: Start at the top-left corner, then extend right by w and down by h.
concepts.technical: Listing 12.2 converts pixel boxes into normalized coordinates on a [0, 1] square via `scale_box`.
concepts.significance: Normalized boxes don't depend on image resolution.
concepts.misconception: That COCO's x, y is the box centre — it is the top-left corner; YOLO later converts to centres (p.363).

concepts.name: COCO annotation structure
concepts.definition: A JSON file with an `images` list and an `annotations` list; each annotation references an image by `image_id` and has a `bbox` and a `category_id`.
concepts.intuition: Two tables joined by an ID.
concepts.technical: Listing 12.2 builds an ID→image dict and groups annotations per image into `{"boxes", "labels", "path"}` records.
concepts.significance: This per-image grouping is the input format for the rest of the chapter.
concepts.example: `metadata[0]` holds all boxes and labels of one training image and its file path.
concepts.misconception: That every image in `train2017` ends up in `metadata` — only images that have at least one annotation do, since entries are created while looping over annotations.

concepts.name: Aspect-preserving box normalization
concepts.definition: Scaling box coordinates by 1/max(W, H) and offsetting the shorter axis by half the size difference.
concepts.intuition: Place the image in the middle of a square canvas, then measure boxes as fractions of the canvas.
concepts.technical: Equivalent to letterbox padding the image to a max(W,H) square and normalizing by its side.
concepts.significance: Lets later code treat every image as a square without distorting box shapes.
concepts.misconception: That x is divided by width and y by height — both use the same factor.

math.title: The scale_box transformation
math.latex: \begin{aligned} s &= \frac{1}{\max(W, H)} \\ x' &= s\,x + \mathbb{1}[H > W]\,\frac{(H - W)\,s}{2} \\ y' &= s\,y + \mathbb{1}[W > H]\,\frac{(W - H)\,s}{2} \\ w' &= s\,w, \quad h' = s\,h \end{aligned}
math.source_text: scale = 1.0 / max(width, height); x, y, w, h = [v * scale for v in box]; x += (height - width) * scale / 2 if height > width else 0; y += (width - height) * scale / 2 if width > height else 0

variables.meaning: Image width and height in pixels (`image["width"]`, `image["height"]`).
COCO box: top-left corner and size in pixels (`annotation["bbox"]`).
Indicator: 1 if the condition holds, else 0.
Normalized box on the unit square.

math.operations: Uniform scaling of all four values, then a translation of the coordinate along the image's shorter side.
math.purpose: Put all boxes on a common [0, 1] square regardless of image size, without distorting aspect ratio.
math.interpretation: The offset $(H-W)s/2$ (or $(W-H)s/2$) is the width of the padding band on one side if the image is centred in a square of side $\max(W,H)$.
math.intuition: Imagine pasting the photo in the centre of a square sheet; the new coordinates are positions on that sheet measured as fractions of its side.

code.title: Parsing the COCO data
code.original_code:
import json

with open(f"{annotations_path}/annotations/instances_train2017.json", "r") as f:
    annotations = json.load(f)

images = {image["id"]: image for image in annotations["images"]}

def scale_box(box, width, height):
    scale = 1.0 / max(width, height)
    x, y, w, h = [v * scale for v in box]
    x += (height - width) * scale / 2 if height > width else 0
    y += (width - height) * scale / 2 if width > height else 0
    return [x, y, w, h]

metadata = {}
for annotation in annotations["annotations"]:
    id = annotation["image_id"]
    if id not in metadata:
        metadata[id] = {"boxes": [], "labels": []}
    image = images[id]
    box = scale_box(annotation["bbox"], image["width"], image["height"])
    metadata[id]["boxes"].append(box)
    metadata[id]["labels"].append(annotation["category_id"])
    metadata[id]["path"] = images_path + "/train2017/" + image["file_name"]
metadata = list(metadata.values())
code.what_it_does: Loads the COCO training annotations, indexes images by ID, converts every box to normalized unit-square coordinates, and groups boxes and labels per image into a list of records.

line_explanations.explanation: Load the whole `instances_train2017.json` into a Python dict `annotations` (a large file; this takes a while and noticeable memory).

Dict comprehension mapping each image ID to its record (file_name, width, height, …). The callout calls this 'Sorts image metadata by ID'; it is an ID-keyed lookup table, giving O(1) access in the loop.

`scale_box`: one scale factor for both axes; shift x by half the height–width difference for portrait images, or y by half the width–height difference for landscape images. Callout: 'Converts bounding box to coordinates on a unit square'.

Start an empty dict and loop over every annotation; create a new record with empty `boxes` and `labels` lists the first time an image ID is seen. Callout: 'Aggregates all bounding box annotations by image ID'.
Look up the image's size, scale the annotation's `bbox`, and append the box and its `category_id` label.
Store the image's full file path (overwritten with the same value for each annotation of the image).
Keep only the values: `metadata` becomes a list of dicts `{"boxes", "labels", "path"}`, one per annotated image.

code.inputs_outputs: Inputs: `annotations_path`, `images_path`. Output: `metadata`, a list where each element has `boxes` (list of `[x, y, w, h]` floats on the unit square), `labels` (list of integer COCO category IDs) and `path` (JPEG file path).
code.algorithm: Hash join of annotations onto images by ID, with a per-row geometric transformation and grouping.
code.theory_link: Supervised detection needs (image, set of boxes, set of labels) triples; normalized coordinates make the targets independent of image resolution, which matters once images are resized to the model's input size.

pitfalls: `id` shadows Python's built-in `id()` function; harmless here but best avoided.
The normalized coordinates only line up with the pixels if the images are later padded to a square (centred) before resizing; resizing with distortion would misalign boxes.
Images with no annotations never enter `metadata`.

# AI-written check of scale_box on the worked example
print(scale_box([100, 50, 200, 100], width=640, height=480))
# [0.15625, 0.203125, 0.3125, 0.15625]

# Inverse (pixels on the original image), assuming the same padding convention
def unscale_box(box, width, height):
    side = max(width, height)
    x, y, w, h = box
    x -= (height - width) / side / 2 if height > width else 0
    y -= (width - height) / side / 2 if width > height else 0
    return [v * side for v in (x, y, w, h)]

deeper.title: Why one scale factor instead of dividing x by W and y by H?
deeper.body:
Two common normalizations exist (comparison not in the book):

- **Independent**: $x/W$, $y/H$. Every image fills the whole unit square, but if images are then resized to a square input, objects get stretched.
- **Aspect-preserving (used here)**: divide by $\max(W,H)$ and centre. The image occupies a centred rectangle inside the square; the rest is padding. Box shapes are preserved.

The second matches resizing with padding to a square, which keeps object proportions intact — sensible for a detector that must learn box widths and heights.

deeper.title: Tracing the loop on two annotations of the same image
deeper.body:
Suppose annotations `A1 = {image_id: 7, bbox: [...], category_id: 1}` and `A2 = {image_id: 7, bbox: [...], category_id: 19}`.

1. `A1`: 7 not in `metadata` → create `{"boxes": [], "labels": []}`; append scaled box and label 1; set path.
2. `A2`: 7 already present → append second box and label 19; path reassigned to the same string.
3. After the loop: `metadata[7] == {"boxes": [b1, b2], "labels": [1, 19], "path": ".../train2017/<file>"}`.

`list(metadata.values())` then drops the IDs.

misconceptions.claim: COCO's `bbox` [x, y, w, h] gives the box centre.
misconceptions.correction: The page says the coordinates start at the top-left corner of the image; x, y is the box's top-left corner.

misconceptions.claim: `scale_box` divides x by the width and y by the height.
misconceptions.correction: Both axes are divided by max(width, height), and the shorter axis is shifted to centre the image in the square.
It builds a dictionary keyed by image ID for fast lookup, despite the callout's wording.

takeaways: COCO images and annotations come as separate downloads linked by image IDs.
COCO boxes are `x, y, width, height` pixels from the top-left corner.
`scale_box` normalizes boxes to a [0, 1] square using one factor, 1/max(W, H), and centres the shorter side — equivalent to padding the image to a square.
`metadata` is a list of per-image records with `boxes`, `labels` (COCO category IDs) and `path`.
Normalized boxes let later code ignore each image's original size.

questions.question: Using `scale_box`, convert the box [40, 60, 120, 80] on a portrait image of width 300 and height 400.
questions.explanation: Height > width, so x is shifted by half of the width deficit; y is not shifted.

questions.question: What does `images = {image["id"]: image for image in annotations["images"]}` actually do?
options: Sorts the images by file name
Builds a dictionary mapping image IDs to image records
questions.answer: Builds a dictionary mapping image IDs to image records
questions.explanation: It is a dict comprehension keyed by ID, used for lookup in the loop. Nothing is sorted (despite the callout), no pixels are loaded, and no filtering happens on this line.

questions.question: What three keys does each element of `metadata` contain, and what is in each?
questions.answer: `boxes` — the list of normalized [x, y, w, h] boxes; `labels` — the list of COCO category IDs; `path` — the image file path under train2017/.

questions.question: Why does rescaling boxes to a unit square make later code simpler?
questions.answer: Boxes no longer depend on each image's pixel size, so they remain valid after images are resized to a common input size and can be manipulated (e.g. mapped to a grid) without consulting each image's dimensions.
questions.explanation: The page: 'This will make it easier to manipulate these boxes without needing to check the size of each input image.'

questions.question: Why does `scale_box` add an offset to y for a landscape image?
options: To convert the top-left corner into the box centre
Because the image is assumed centred in a square, leaving padding above and below
To flip the y axis upward
questions.answer: Because the image is assumed centred in a square, leaving padding above and below
questions.explanation: The offset equals half the width–height difference (scaled), the height of the top padding band. Centre conversion happens later (p.363); there is no axis flip; compression is irrelevant.

questions.question: Would an image in `train2017` that has no annotations appear in `metadata`? Why?
questions.answer: No. Records are created only while iterating over annotations, so an image with none is never added.
questions.explanation: Follows from the structure of the loop in listing 12.2.

questions.question: Can you write the inverse of `scale_box` to recover pixel coordinates?
questions.answer: Subtract the same centring offset, then multiply by max(width, height).
questions.explanation: See the illustrative `unscale_box` in the code notes.
